Language across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Between ages 5 and 7 children’s language explodes in both breadth and complexity. Receptive vocabulary on the order of ten thousand words is typical by age five and children learn thousands more words each year 1, with expressive repertoires expanding to include not just concrete nouns and action verbs but metacognitive verbs (remember, conclude, decide) and metalinguistic verbs (explain, confirm) that describe thinking and communication itself 2, 3, alongside abstract descriptive terms (carefully, slowly, surprised) and relational words that go beyond the basic spatial prepositions of earlier years 3. Vocabulary growth reflects not just breadth but richer semantic networks (e.g., learning multiple related senses of the same word) that support inference during reading 4. Children this age also transition from predominantly concrete word learning to systematic acquisition of abstract terms (love, freedom, success), reflecting the cognitive demands of formal schooling. A small study examines language and shared reading (Figure) 10.

Syntactic complexity undergoes a measurable inflection: whereas five-year-olds produce mostly simple sentences punctuated by coordinate clauses joined with "and" or "but", six- and seven-year-olds show steep increases in subordination, with conditional clauses (if) appearing reliably by ages 6-7, relative pronouns (e.g the scientist "who discovered penicillin") and embedded subordinate clauses (e.g she believes "that the experiment will succeed") rising between 7-8, and the proportion of utterances containing subordinate clauses climbing roughly 0.2% per month across the elementary years 5, 6, 7; children increasingly deploy advanced conjunctions (because, so, while, although, unless) to link ideas causally and temporally within single utterances, yielding longer, hierarchically structured sentences that can express conditionality, contrast, and multi-clause logical relations 6, 3, 7. Receptive sophistication keeps pace: children reliably follow multi-step unrelated commands, understand that words can have multiple meanings (e.g orange the fruit vs. the color) and that different words can mean the same thing (e.g minus and take away), and track stories told over multiple days without losing the thread 3, all while their processing speed for familiar words accelerates and their ability to extract meaning from increasingly complex syntactic frames improves markedly.

Narrative capabilities also transform dramatically. Five-year-olds produce primitive narratives with basic story grammar elements but limited temporal sequencing and causal coherence, relying heavily on "and" as their primary connector. By age 7, children consistently include 5+ story grammar elements (character, setting, initiating event, action, consequences, resolution) 8 with logical temporal ordering and appropriate causal markers, although the inclusion of multiple episodes with reliable causal chaining and rich "inner state" descriptions of agents appears to remain mostly out of reach. A preschool study examines narrative comprehension (Figure) 9.
